featured_videos.title: The Carnivore Calorie Myth That Could Stall Fat Loss
featured_videos.creator: Jenny Mitich
featured_videos.editorial_title: The Carnivore Calorie Myth That Could Stall Fat Loss
featured_videos.commentary: Here's the thing: the comment about calorie counting destroying someone's progress for 50 years hits different when you realize most of us were never taught to trust our own hunger signals in the first place. Jenny's right that a calorie isn't a calorie, but what's wild is watching people in the comments split into two camps: the ones who ditched counting entirely and felt better, and the ones who needed to *count up* because they were undereating at 1400 calories. The real myth isn't that calories don't matter. It's that one approach works for everyone. Some people find that tracking keeps them honest and consistent for years. Others break free the moment they stop obsessing and start listening. Both are valid. This is why breaking a weight loss stall isn't always about eating less, sometimes it's about eating more and giving your body permission to relax.

featured_videos.title: The BBC Got the Carnivore Diet WRONG: Here's Why
featured_videos.creator: The Primal Lifestyle
featured_videos.editorial_title: The BBC Got the Carnivore Diet WRONG: Here's Why
featured_videos.commentary: The comment about six years without fiber and better digestion pretty much sums up why mainstream media struggles with carnivore, right? They're working from a playbook that says fiber is non-negotiable, so when people show up with better digestion, clearer skin, and stable energy, it doesn't fit the narrative. What Carl's pointing out here isn't conspiracy thinking, it's just asking why self-reported health improvements from thousands of people get dismissed as anecdotal while a studio doctor's theoretical concerns get treated as gospel. The real frustration in these comments isn't about media bias per se, it's that people have actually fixed their health problems, and instead of curious questions, they get lectured about carbohydrates being essential when. as someone mentioned. there literally aren't any essential carbohydrates. That's not opinion, that's biochemistry.

featured_videos.title: I Got My Test Results Back...and it's not good
featured_videos.creator: Carnivore Quest
featured_videos.editorial_title: I Got My Test Results Back.and it's not good
featured_videos.commentary: The community showed up for Larry in a real way here, and that matters more than you might think. What struck me was how many people shared their own lung healing stories, not as cheerleading but as proof this isn't hopeless. One person quit smoking and can't even tell they were a smoker anymore. Another's mother-in-law reversed severe COPD with keto. That's not motivation theater, that's data from real lives. Weight loss on carnivore isn't just about the number on the scale anymore for Larry, it's about oxygen and breathing and getting back to normal, and honestly, that kind of clarity can be the difference between sticking with it and falling off. The fact that this community knows his story, knows what he's been through, and still showed up with prayer and fasting advice and hope, tells me everything about why people stay in this space.

featured_videos.title: I Lost 130 lbs. Carnivore Is NOT the Answer.
featured_videos.creator: Chris Cooking Nashville
featured_videos.editorial_title: I Lost 130 lbs. Carnivore Is NOT the Answer.
featured_videos.commentary: Chris nails something most diet content misses: the actual problem isn't which foods you eat, it's the relationship you have with yourself. The comments are full of people saying "I finally feel worthy" and "my family is worth it," and that's where the real transformation happens. Carnivore worked for Chris because it gave him a tool to interrupt the dopamine chase, but that same tool won't work for someone who hasn't addressed the underlying belief that they deserve to feel good. The diet is just the vehicle. If you're thinking carnivore is your savior, you're setting yourself up for the same cycle he's describing. Start with the belief that you're worth taking care of, then pick whatever eating strategy actually sticks for you.

featured_videos.title: Most Carnivores are WRONG About Fat
featured_videos.creator: HomeSteadHow
featured_videos.editorial_title: Most Carnivores are WRONG About Fat
featured_videos.commentary: Most carnivores do treat fat like it's all the same, and the comments here show why that matters. Someone mentioned buying hard white beef fat from ranches and frying it until brown. that's the opposite of what people usually do with soft intramuscular fat, and the results speak for themselves. The picanha method in an air fryer straight from frozen is genius because you're actually controlling how the different fat layers behave. Here's the thing: fat quality and how you cook it changes digestion, satiety, and how your body actually uses it. Stop guessing about ratios and start paying attention to how different cuts and cooking methods make you feel. your digestion will tell you everything you need to know.

featured_videos.title: The Mediterranean diet VS the Carnivore diet.  Nick Norwitz is wrong again.
featured_videos.creator: Haircafe
featured_videos.editorial_title: The Mediterranean diet VS the Carnivore diet.  Nick Norwitz is wrong again.
featured_videos.commentary: Look, the comment about dropouts hits on something nobody talks about: study design matters way more than most people realize. When a diet is so unappetizing that people bail or start cheating, the results don't actually tell you anything about the diet itself. That's exactly what happened here with the Mediterranean group. The carnivore folks stuck with it because they felt good, which is the whole point. Nick Norwitz keeps missing that distinction, and it's frustrating to watch. If you're curious about how carnivore compares to other diets from an actual research lens, Kevin's breaking down what the data actually shows versus what makes for clickable headlines.
